content: The national prevalence of early warning indicators (EWIs) can be estimated by combining data from randomly sampled clinics and conveniently sampled clinics. This approach allows for the calculation of a representative national prevalence while incorporating data from clinics with readily available information. Random sampling ensures that the results are representative of the country as a whole, while conveniently sampled clinics can provide additional data without compromising representativeness. Primary sampling refers to the selection of clinics, while secondary sampling involves selecting patients within those clinics. Ideally, EWIs should be reported annually from all antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinics in a country. However, in cases where this is not feasible, a progressive, multi-year scale-up approach is recommended. For example, a country may begin by sampling 20% of clinics in the first year, then expand coverage by an additional 20% each year until all clinics are reporting by the fifth year. This gradual expansion ensures comprehensive monitoring over time. Clinics can be selected using a combination of random sampling and convenience sampling. Clinics that have historically reported EWIs or have readily available data, such as those with electronic medical records (EMRs), should continue to be included in the sample. However, random sampling should remain the primary method of clinic selection to maintain national representativeness. Representative sampling can be achieved through simple random sampling or stratified random sampling, such as by district or province. Secondary sampling involves collecting patient-level data within clinics. Whenever possible, data should be abstracted for all eligible patients (a census). If a census is not feasible, a sample of patients can be selected to ensure results are generalizable to the entire eligible population at the clinic. The sample size for secondary sampling is determined based on the size of the eligible patient population for each EWI. For example, the eligible population for on-time ARV drug pick-up may include all pediatric patients receiving ART, while retention on ART may focus on a cohort of adult patients who initiated ART during a specific reporting period. Sample size calculations are designed to achieve 95% confidence intervals with a margin of error of ±7%. Once the required sample size is determined, consecutive patient records are sampled until the target is reached. Clinics are encouraged to use tools developed by the World Health Organization (WHO) to facilitate data abstraction and ensure accurate reporting. After data abstraction, each clinic calculates the EWIs and assigns classifications based on thresholds (e.g., red, amber, green). A grey classification is used if ≥30% of data is missing. It is not necessary to calculate confidence intervals for EWI classifications. At the national level, countries should report the proportion of clinics achieving each classification for each indicator and patient population (adult and pediatric). This allows program managers to identify areas of need and monitor improvements or declines over time. Nationally representative prevalence estimates for each EWI can be calculated by aggregating and weighting data from sampled clinics. Clinics with larger patient populations are weighted more heavily than smaller clinics. However, aggregation should only be performed if data availability exceeds 70% for the nationally eligible population monitored by a specific indicator. If less than 70% of data is available, aggregation should not be performed. Conveniently sampled clinics can be included in national estimates if they represent more than 70% of the eligible patient population for each indicator. A flowchart is provided to assess the feasibility of data aggregation at the national level. For paper-based medical records, clinics must ensure accurate data abstraction and reporting to maintain the integrity of the monitoring system.
